answers.text: I would tell the assistant: give exactly three lines every time — drop-off time, pallet count, damage noted, in that order. Anything else in the message can be left out.
List each call with time, customer, topic and outcome in that order, then count as a follow-up any call where the outcome shows the issue is still open.
Looking at the times again, something does not add up between when the crew starts and when the note says they finish — I think that is the part to flag, though I am not fully sure why.
118 against 96 last month — I had a quick look at that but I am not sure the percentage is quite right.
I would go with the second one — 827 out of 940 written out, not just the 88% on its own.
I would send the second email, it has the actual volume numbers in it — the first one just says 'better rate' without anything behind it to check.
1. No. 2. Yes. 3. No, not released yet. 4. Yes, already public. 5. No.

The hourly rates and retainer cap I would leave out of anything I paste in — those numbers are exactly what makes this client's deal different from others, so that stays internal. The confidentiality clause worries me too, since it names our company and the client by name, which is not something I want floating in a tool we have not checked properly.
Before it goes to whoever needs the summary, I would check the totals against the stock count sheet myself.
Step one is where I would watch first, since a misread invoice carries through. But step four is the one that worries me more, since it submits on its own without anyone looking.
